text: PJM = PJM Interconnection; SPP = Southwest Power Pool Unlike merchant transmission projects—where transmission costs are paid by interconnecting generator-customers with negotiated service agreements—regionally planned transmission project costs are allocated to project beneficiaries. Determining who benefits from a project can be challenging because the benefits of a high-voltage transmission project are often distributed across a broad geographic area and a diverse set of network users. Further, the benefits and beneficiaries of a transmission project change over the multidecadal lifetime of the project. As a result, there is generally no single network user willing to pay for a regional project because they would receive only a fraction of the benefits. Across the United States, different regions have developed a multitude of cost allocation methods designed to assign costs to project beneficiaries. Legal disputes over the methods used to calculate project benefits have led to litigation between utilities, regulators, and customer groups. In this report, we evaluate what factors influence successful transmission cost allocation agreements and identify lessons learned to minimize cost allocation disputes for future projects. These findings will inform potential opportunities for federal, regional, and state regulators and project developers to reduce cost allocation barriers for bulk transmission development. 1.1 Regulatory and Legal Background of Transmission Cost Allocation Transmission cost allocation is the assignment of costs among network users for building and operating a transmission facility. These costs are ultimately paid by the end consumer through direct charges on ratepayer bills or in the form of higher per-unit energy rates. The objectives of transmission charges are to guarantee cost recovery for prudent network investments and to send efficient locational signals to network users regarding the costs of installing their facilities in 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. different parts of the grid (Olmos 2013). In Order 1000, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) requires that transmission costs “must be allocated to those within the transmission planning region that benefit from those facilities in a manner that is at least roughly commensurate with benefits” (FERC 2011). Order 1000 was purposefully designed to allow transmission providers flexibility to develop their own cost allocation methods in accordance with this “beneficiary pays” principle. As a result, there exist a variety of transmission cost allocation methods across the United States. The beneficiary pays principle is a simple concept—ubiquitous in cost-of-service rate regulation —that is difficult to implement in practice.1 Although transmission costs are usually well defined, the benefits of a transmission facility are more difficult to quantify. There is no universal catalog of transmission benefits. Chang, Pfeifenberger, and Hagerty developed a comprehensive list of transmission benefits, including more than 30 possible items (Chang et al. 2013). The challenge, as their list demonstrates, is that some benefits (e.g., production cost savings) are relatively straightforward to measure but others (e.g., increased market liquidity, improved reliability) are difficult to measure and quantify.
